prompt: `java -jar target/bookshop-0.1.0.jar` starts. Which class does the JVM run first?
hint: The JVM reads one attribute of the manifest and nothing else.

choices.text: `BookshopApplication`, the class with `@SpringBootApplication`
choices.why: That is `Start-Class`, an attribute the JVM does not know about. The launcher reads it and calls its `main` once the libraries can be loaded.

choices.text: `JarLauncher`, from Spring Boot's loader
choices.why: `Main-Class` names it. It builds a class loader that can read the jars inside the jar, then hands over to `Start-Class`.

choices.text: Tomcat's bootstrap class, which deploys the application into the server
choices.why: Tomcat is one of the libraries in `BOOT-INF/lib`. The application starts it, and not the other way round.

choices.text: A Maven class that resolves the dependencies listed in `pom.xml`
choices.why: Maven has finished its work when the jar exists. Every library is already inside the file, and the server needs no Maven.

prompt: Why are the jars under `BOOT-INF/lib` stored without compression?
hint: Think about what the launcher does with them at start-up.

choices.text: Because the zip format cannot hold a compressed file inside another compressed file
choices.why: It can; a zip of zips is ordinary. Storing is a choice Boot makes, for a reason that has to do with reading.

choices.text: So the launcher can read each one in place, without unpacking it first
choices.why: A stored entry is the original bytes at a known offset, so a nested jar can be opened directly inside the outer file.

choices.text: So the JVM's own class loader can put them on the class path
choices.why: The JVM's class loader cannot load a jar inside a jar at all, stored or not. That gap is the reason the launcher exists.

choices.text: To make the executable jar smaller
choices.why: Storing never makes a file smaller. A jar is already compressed inside, so little is lost by not compressing it again.

prompt: A colleague copies `bookshop-0.1.0.jar.original` to a server, because it is smaller, and runs `java -jar` on it. What happens?
hint: Compare what each of the two files holds.

choices.text: It starts as before, because the libraries are fetched from Maven Central on the first run
choices.why: Nothing in a jar downloads anything. A plain jar is only its own classes, and the libraries have to be on the class path some other way.

choices.text: It refuses to start, because that jar has no `Main-Class` attribute
choices.why: The plain jar Maven built first has the bookshop's own classes and no launcher, and its manifest names no class to run.

choices.text: It starts and fails at the first request, when a Spring class is missing
choices.why: It never gets as far as a request: `java -jar` needs a main class before anything runs.

choices.text: It starts, because `.original` is only a backup copy of the same file
choices.why: They differ by a factor of over a thousand in size. The `.original` is what Maven built before Boot's plugin repackaged it.

prompt: Spring Boot binds the environment variable `___` to the property `management.server.address`.
hint: Relaxed binding: dots become underscores, letters become capitals.

prompt: The jar's `application.properties` says `spring.datasource.username=bookshop`, and the shell that starts it has `SPRING_DATASOURCE_USERNAME=shop` exported. Which user does the application log in to PostgreSQL as?
hint: Lesson 4 ranked the places a property can come from.

choices.text: `bookshop`, because the file is packaged with the code and wins over the machine
choices.why: It is the other way round: the file inside the jar is one of the weakest places, so that the machine can override it.

choices.text: `shop`
choices.why: An environment variable outranks `application.properties`, and relaxed binding maps the variable onto that very property.

choices.text: Neither: Spring Boot refuses to start when two places set the same property
choices.why: Two places setting one property is the normal case, and the order decides it without a word in the log.

choices.text: `bookshop`, because a username, unlike a password, is never read from the environment
choices.why: Binding does not care what a property means. Every property can be set from the environment.

prompt: A team keeps the production database password in `application-prod.properties`, inside the jar, and only switches the profile on the server. What is the problem with that?
hint: Who can read a jar?

choices.text: A profile's file is ignored once the jar is built
choices.why: It is read: lesson 4 started the bookshop with the `dev` profile from a built jar.

choices.text: Anybody who copies the jar reads the password with `unzip -p`, and changing it means a new build
choices.why: A jar is a zip file. The password travels with every copy of the artefact, to every registry and laptop, and rotating it is a release.

choices.text: A password must always be given on the command line, which outranks every file
choices.why: The command line outranks it, but a password there can be read by every user who lists the machine's processes. The environment is the usual place.

choices.text: Spring Boot encrypts properties files in the jar, so the password would be unreadable to the application
choices.why: Nothing is encrypted: `unzip -p` prints the file as it was written.

prompt: Of the four layers the jar is split into, which one changes with almost every commit?
hint: Where do your own classes go?

choices.text: `dependencies`
choices.why: It changes when the `pom.xml` changes a library, which is far rarer than a change to the code.

choices.text: `spring-boot-loader`
choices.why: The launcher changes when Spring Boot is upgraded, and at no other time.

choices.text: `snapshot-dependencies`
choices.why: It holds libraries whose version ends in `-SNAPSHOT`, and the bookshop has none, so it is empty.

choices.text: `application`
choices.why: `BOOT-INF/classes` is there, with the bookshop's classes, its properties and its migrations.

prompt: The bookshop starts depending on a library at version `2.1.0-SNAPSHOT`. Where does `extract --layers` put it?
hint: Read `layers.idx` against the version.

choices.text: In `dependencies`, with every other library
choices.why: A snapshot can change without changing its version, so Boot keeps it out of the layer that is meant to stay still.

choices.text: In `snapshot-dependencies`, a layer of its own
choices.why: That layer exists for exactly this: a library whose bytes may change on any build, kept apart so it does not invalidate the big stable one.

choices.text: In `application`, because a snapshot is code still under development
choices.why: `application` is the project's own output. A snapshot from somewhere else still goes to a layer for libraries.

choices.text: Nowhere: snapshot versions are refused by the repackage
choices.why: They are accepted; the empty `snapshot-dependencies` directory is waiting for one.

prompt: Match each layer to what makes it change.
hint: The order the Dockerfile copies them in is the same idea.

pairs.right: a library added or upgraded in pom.xml
a new version of Spring Boot
a change to the bookshop's code

prompt: Why does the Dockerfile start `FROM eclipse-temurin:25-jre-noble` rather than from `ubuntu:24.04` with a line that installs Java?
hint: What is `noble`, and what is a JRE?

choices.text: Because Ubuntu's archive does not carry Java 25
choices.why: It does: lesson 1 installed `openjdk-25-jdk` from it. The base image is a matter of who maintains the layer, not of availability.

choices.text: It is the same Ubuntu 24.04 with a Java 25 runtime already installed and kept up to date by its maintainers
choices.why: `noble` is Ubuntu 24.04's name, and the `jre` tag carries a runtime without the compiler. Nobody has to write or maintain the install.

choices.text: Because only that image can run a Spring Boot jar
choices.why: Any image with a Java 25 runtime runs it. This one is a convenient, maintained choice.

choices.text: Because a JRE image includes `curl`, which the health check needs
choices.why: It does not: `command -v` found no `curl` in it, which is why the health check uses `bash` alone.

prompt: Put the four `COPY` lines of the second stage in the order the Dockerfile uses.
hint: Least often changed first.
trap: Copying `application` earlier would make every code change rebuild the layers after it, the 69 MB of libraries included.

prompt: After the one-word change to `CatalogueReport` and a new `docker build`, how many lines did `diff` print as changed in the list of the image's layers, counting only the lines starting with `>`?
hint: Each layer is one line of that list.

prompt: Somebody reorders the Dockerfile so that `application` is copied first and `dependencies` last. Every image still works. What gets worse?
hint: A layer is reused only if every layer below it was reused too.

choices.text: Nothing: Docker compares each layer's content, so the order of the `COPY` lines does not matter
choices.why: Each layer is stacked on the one below it, and a changed layer invalidates everything above it, whatever its content.

choices.text: Every code change produces a new 69 MB layer of libraries, to be stored and pushed again
choices.why: The code layer now sits at the bottom of the four, so every layer above it is rebuilt, and the biggest one is among them.

choices.text: The application starts more slowly, because the launcher finds its classes last
choices.why: At run time the four directories are merged into one `/app`; the order of the layers is invisible to the JVM.

choices.text: The image gets bigger, because each layer then stores a copy of the ones below
choices.why: A layer stores only what it adds. The size of one image is the same; what grows is what changes between two of them.

prompt: What does `USER bookshop` in the second stage change? Choose all that apply.
hint: `docker run --entrypoint id` answered the question for one of them.

choices.text: The Java process in the container runs as uid 10001, not as root
choices.why: `ENTRYPOINT` runs as the last `USER` named, and `ps` inside the container showed it.

choices.text: The `RUN` lines after it run as that user
choices.why: Every instruction that runs a command uses the current user, which is why `useradd` sits before `USER` and not after it.

choices.text: The files the `COPY` lines put in `/app` belong to `bookshop`
choices.why: `COPY` gives files to root unless it is told otherwise with `--chown`, whatever `USER` says. That is fine here: the application only needs to read them.

choices.text: Only the host's `bookshop` user may start the container
choices.why: `USER` is about the process inside. Who may start containers on the host is decided by access to Docker's socket, as lesson 19 set up.

prompt: In `compose.yaml`, the bookshop's `SPRING_DATASOURCE_URL` names the host `db`. Why would `localhost` not work in its place?
hint: Each container has its own network interfaces.

choices.text: Because PostgreSQL refuses connections that come from `localhost`
choices.why: PostgreSQL accepts them happily. The connection would never reach PostgreSQL in the first place.

choices.text: Because `localhost` in a container is that container, and the database runs in another one
choices.why: On the network Compose creates, each service is reached by its name, and `db` resolves to the database container's address.

choices.text: Because `localhost` would reach the PostgreSQL that lesson 9 installed on the machine
choices.why: The machine's loopback is not the container's. From inside, `localhost` reaches neither database.

choices.text: Because the port 5432 is not published in `compose.yaml`
choices.why: Publishing is for reaching a container from outside. Containers on the same Compose network reach each other's ports without it.

prompt: Match each line of `compose.yaml` to what it guarantees.
hint: Read the notes beside the file.

pairs.right: the application starts after PostgreSQL answers
the catalogue survives docker compose down
the management port is reachable only from the machine itself
nothing starts while the secret is missing

right_distractors: the container restarts after a crash

prompt: Which command removes the containers and also deletes the catalogue PostgreSQL keeps?
hint: The data lives in a named volume.

choices.text: `docker compose stop`
choices.why: It stops the containers and keeps them, ready to start again with everything in place.

choices.text: `docker compose down`
choices.why: It removes the containers and the network and keeps the volume, which is why the second start found the schema up to date.

choices.text: `docker compose down -v`
choices.why: `-v` removes the named volumes the file declares as well, and with `db-data` goes every row.

choices.text: `docker compose rm`
choices.why: It removes stopped containers only. Volumes are left alone.

prompt: You delete the line `MANAGEMENT_SERVER_ADDRESS: 0.0.0.0` and start the stack again. What happens?
hint: Where does the health check run, and where does your `curl` run?

choices.text: The container never becomes healthy, because the health check cannot reach port 8081
choices.why: The health check runs inside the container, where 127.0.0.1 is exactly the address the management server now listens on.

choices.text: Port 8080 stops answering too, because both ports share one setting
choices.why: `management.server.address` belongs to the management server alone; the API keeps listening on every interface.

choices.text: The container reports healthy, and a `curl` to 127.0.0.1:8081 from the machine fails
choices.why: The management server falls back to the 127.0.0.1 in `application.properties`, the container's own loopback, which a published port does not reach.

choices.text: Nothing changes, because the published port already limits 8081 to the machine
choices.why: The two limits are on different sides. The published port decides who outside may connect; the address decides where inside the server listens.

prompt: `docker compose stop app` returned in under a second, and the container's exit code was 143. What does 143 say?
hint: 128 plus a signal's number.

choices.text: The JVM crashed while closing the connection pool
choices.why: The log showed the pool's `Shutdown completed.` before the exit. A crash would leave a stack trace instead.

choices.text: Docker killed the process after waiting ten seconds
choices.why: That is 137, 128 plus SIGKILL's 9, and the shell-form detour shows it.

choices.text: The process ended because of SIGTERM, after running its shutdown hooks
choices.why: 15 is SIGTERM. The JVM ran Spring's graceful shutdown, then exited with the code that says which signal ended it.

choices.text: An error in the application, which should be read in the log
choices.why: A code above 128 names a signal rather than an error. This one is the ordinary end of a Java process asked to stop.

prompt: The JVM option that sets the maximum heap as a share of the container's memory limit is `-XX:___=75`.
hint: The default is 25.

prompt: A container is given `--memory=2g`, and the JVM in it is started with `-XX:MaxRAMPercentage=75`. What maximum heap does the JVM choose, in MiB?
hint: 2g is 2048 MiB.

prompt: You fixed a bug in `BookService`. Put the steps that get the fix running in Compose in order.
hint: The image is built from the jar, not from the source.
items: docker build replaces only the application layer
docker compose up -d replaces the app container
the readiness check reports UP and the container turns healthy
trap: Building the image before `mvn package` copies the OLD jar in, and the new image runs the bug you just fixed.

prompt: The same image is to run on a test server and in production. Which of these belong in the environment rather than in the image? Choose all that apply.
hint: What differs between the two places, and what must not be readable from the image?

choices.text: The database URL
choices.why: Each place has its own database. One image with the URL in the environment runs against either.

choices.text: The token-signing secret
choices.why: A secret in an image is readable by anybody who can pull it, and both places would then sign with the same key.

choices.text: The libraries in `BOOT-INF/lib`
choices.why: They are what was tested. Supplying them per place would make the test server and production run different code.

choices.text: The user the process runs as
choices.why: It is a property of how the image was built, the same everywhere, and nothing about it is secret.

prompt: A colleague's image starts `java -jar app.jar` with no memory options at all, and it runs with `--memory=512m`. How big may its heap grow?
hint: The JVM reads the limit, and the default share is a quarter.

choices.text: A quarter of the server's physical memory, because the JVM does not see the container's limit
choices.why: The JVM has read the limit for years: with `--memory=1g` it chose 256 MiB, not a quarter of the 15 GB machine.

choices.text: 512 MiB, the whole limit
choices.why: The whole limit leaves nothing for metaspace, threads and the JIT's code, and the kernel would kill the container first.

choices.text: 128 MiB
choices.why: 25% of 512 MiB. For a Spring Boot application that is tight, which is why the bookshop's image sets 75%.

choices.text: 256 MiB, the default heap whatever the limit
choices.why: 256 MiB was a quarter of the 1 GiB limit in the lesson, not a fixed default: the heap follows the limit.
